# Chángé walks into a space, astronomy & celestial science firm

Somewhere right now, in a space, astronomy & celestial science office, someone is doing exactly what the myths describe — and has never heard of **Chángé**. This file is the introduction.

## Before the Office, the Story

**The Elixir of Immortality.** The core myth, fixed in the Huáinánzǐ (c.  2nd century BCE), begins with the archer Hòuyì, who had shot down nine of the ten suns and so received from Xīwángmǔ, Queen Mother of the West, the elixir of immortality.  Chángé took it and floated up to the moon, where she became its goddess.

**From Héng'é to Chángé.** The goddess was originally 姮娥 Héng'é.  Under the Han, her name was altered to avoid the naming taboo on the personal name of Emperor Wen, Liú Héng 劉恆: the graph 姮 was replaced by the synonymous 常, and Héng'é became Chángé.  It is a rare case where imperial censorship is legible inside a divine name itself — a goddess renamed so that a mortal emperor's name could remain unspoken.

## The Reveal, Seat by Seat

### Space, Astronomy & Celestial Science

Now read the why-line with the office in mind: *China's lunar exploration program flies her name — the Chang'e orbiters and sample-return landers are the moon goddess made mission architecture.* The people doing this work did not borrow the archetype. They re-derived it — the way Chángé was always going to be re-derived wherever moon, immortality, mid-autumn matters.

### Faith & Spiritual Organizations

*The Mid-Autumn moon altar is still set for her each year — mooncakes, incense, and the goddess in the full moon.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

### Food & Hospitality

*The mooncake is her festival's edible icon — an entire pastry economy rises with her moon each autumn.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

## Not the First Rebrand

The rabbit in the moon is older than any single nation's telling of it.  Buddhist tradition carried the śaśajātaka — the tale of the rabbit who offered itself as food and was set in the moon as a reward — from India into East Asia, and scholars commonly link the Chinese moon rabbit to this transmission, though the Jade Rabbit's elixir-pounding is China's own elaboration. The office is only the latest translation.
